q: You're driving a car on a single carriageway road and pass this sign. What's the maximum speed you can now drive at?
options: 50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
40 mph
explain: This sign means the national speed limit applies. For cars on a single carriageway that's 60 mph, but you should still drive at a speed that suits the conditions.

q: You're driving a car on a dual carriageway where the national speed limit applies. What's the maximum speed limit?
options: 60 mph
50 mph
80 mph
70 mph
explain: The national speed limit for cars on a dual carriageway is 70 mph. It's the absolute maximum, not a target.

q: Some rules in the Highway Code use the words 'MUST' or 'MUST NOT'. What does this tell you?
options: They're only good advice
They apply only to learners
They apply only on motorways
They're legal requirements
explain: Rules that use 'MUST' or 'MUST NOT' are legal requirements. If you disobey them you're committing a criminal offence, and you may be fined, get penalty points, be disqualified or, in the most serious cases, be sent to prison.

q: You're turning right at a crossroads. An oncoming vehicle is also turning right. Which way of turning is generally safer?
options: Right side to right side
Left side to left side
Whichever lets you go first
Cutting the corner to turn sooner
explain: Turning right side to right side, keeping the other vehicle on your right and turning behind it, is generally safer as you have a clear view of approaching traffic. Turning left side to left side can block your view of oncoming vehicles.

q: You're driving in England on a road with street lights. There are no signs showing a different speed limit. What limit generally applies?
options: 20 mph
40 mph
50 mph
30 mph
explain: In England and Scotland a 30 mph limit generally applies to roads with street lights (excluding motorways) unless signs show otherwise.

q: You're driving in Wales along a road with street lights. No signs show a different speed limit. What's the speed limit?
options: 30 mph
20 mph
40 mph
50 mph
explain: In Wales a 20 mph limit generally applies to roads with street lights unless signs show otherwise. In England and Scotland it's generally 30 mph.

q: You're following a coach along a single carriageway road where the national speed limit applies. What's the coach's maximum speed limit?
options: 40 mph
60 mph
50 mph
70 mph
explain: Buses, coaches and minibuses are limited to 50 mph on single carriageways, lower than the 60 mph limit for cars. Be patient, as larger vehicles are subject to lower speed limits.

q: You're driving on a country road where the national speed limit applies. It's raining and there are sharp bends ahead. What should you remember about the speed limit?
options: It's the absolute maximum, not a target
It's the speed you should aim to keep to
It only applies when the road is dry
It may be exceeded briefly to overtake
explain: The speed limit is the absolute maximum and doesn't mean it's safe to drive at that speed. You should reduce your speed where there are hazards such as bends, and when the weather makes it safer to do so.

q: You're driving along a two-lane dual carriageway. Which lane should you normally use?
options: The right-hand lane
Whichever lane is less busy
The left-hand lane
The lane with faster traffic
explain: On a two-lane dual carriageway you should stay in the left-hand lane. Use the right-hand lane for overtaking or turning right, then move back to the left when it's safe.

q: You're on a single carriageway road with three lanes. No signs or markings give priority to either direction. What should you use the middle lane for?
options: Driving at a steady speed
Pulling in to let others pass
Turning left into side roads
Overtaking or turning right
explain: Use the middle lane only for overtaking or turning right. You have no more right to use it than a driver coming from the opposite direction, and you shouldn't use the right-hand lane.

q: You're driving in the left-hand lane of a busy multi-lane road and need to move into the right-hand lane. What should you do first?
options: Signal and move across straight away
Check your mirrors and blind spot
Sound your horn to warn other drivers
Brake so that traffic behind can pass
explain: Before changing lane, use your mirrors and, if necessary, take a quick sideways glance to make sure you won't force anyone to change course or speed. Then signal and move over when it's clear.

q: You're driving along a one-way street with two lanes. You want to turn right at the end. Unless signs or markings show otherwise, which lane should you use?
options: The left-hand lane
Either lane
The right-hand lane
The lane with less traffic
explain: In a one-way street you should use the right-hand lane when going right and the left-hand lane when going left, unless signs or markings show otherwise. Choose the correct lane as soon as you can.

q: You're going straight ahead along a busy one-way street with several lanes. What should you be aware of?
options: Traffic could pass you on both sides
Overtaking isn't allowed in one-way streets
You must stay in the left-hand lane
Cyclists aren't allowed to use the street
explain: When going straight ahead in a one-way street, use the most appropriate lane and remember that traffic could be passing on both sides. Don't change lanes suddenly.

q: You're driving along a town road with a bus lane on your left. Signs show it's in operation and don't allow other vehicles. When may you enter it?
options: To get past slow-moving traffic
To stop, load or unload if allowed
When no buses can be seen behind you
To overtake a cyclist in your lane
explain: Unless signs show otherwise, you shouldn't drive in a bus lane during its period of operation. You may enter it to stop, load or unload where this isn't prohibited.

q: You're driving on a road with a cycle lane marked by a solid white line. It's during the lane's times of operation. What must you do?
options: Drive in it only if it's empty
Park in it for no more than 20 minutes
Use it to pass queuing traffic
Not drive or park in it
explain: You MUST NOT drive or park in a cycle lane marked by a solid white line during its times of operation. If it's marked by a broken line, don't drive or park in it unless it's unavoidable.

q: You're approaching a lane shown by this sign. It's within the times shown. Which vehicles may use the lane?
options: Any car that isn't towing a trailer or caravan
Only vehicles with just one person inside
Vehicles carrying the minimum number shown
Only lorries and other large goods vehicles
explain: When a high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lane is in operation it MUST only be used by vehicles carrying at least the minimum number of people shown on the signs, and by other vehicles, such as buses, that the signs allow.

q: You're driving in a city where trams run along some streets. A lane ahead is reserved for trams. What does the Highway Code say about entering it?
options: You must not enter it
You may use it to overtake
You may use it outside peak hours
You may use it if no tram is coming
explain: You MUST NOT enter a road, lane or other route reserved for trams. Take extra care where trams run along the road, and don't follow them when they leave the main carriageway.

q: You're approaching a roundabout. There are no signs, road markings or traffic lights telling you otherwise. Which traffic should you give priority to?
options: Traffic approaching from your left
Traffic waiting to join behind you
Traffic heading for your exit
Traffic approaching from your right
explain: When you reach a roundabout you should give priority to traffic approaching from your right, unless signs, road markings or traffic lights direct otherwise.

q: You're going to take the first exit to the left at a roundabout. Unless signs or markings show otherwise, how should you approach?
options: Signal right and use the right-hand lane
Signal left and use the left-hand lane
Give no signal and use either lane
Signal left and use the right-hand lane
explain: For the first exit, signal left and approach in the left-hand lane. Keep to the left on the roundabout and continue signalling left to leave.

q: You're going to take an exit to the right at a roundabout. There are no signs or markings telling you otherwise. What should you do?
options: Signal left and approach in the left-hand lane
Approach in the left-hand lane with no signal
Signal right and approach in the right-hand lane
Signal right and approach in the left-hand lane
explain: When taking an exit to the right, signal right and approach in the right-hand lane. Keep to the right on the roundabout until you need to change lanes to exit, and signal left after you've passed the exit before the one you want.

q: You're going straight ahead at a roundabout, using an exit between the first and the last. When should you signal left?
options: As you approach the roundabout
As soon as you join the roundabout
You don't need to signal at all
After passing the exit before yours
explain: For an intermediate exit you won't normally need to signal on approach. Stay in your lane and signal left after you've passed the exit before the one you want.

q: You're driving a car and approaching a mini-roundabout. The road is quiet. What must you do?
options: Pass round the central markings
Drive over the central markings
Give way to traffic from your left
Signal right whichever exit you take
explain: All vehicles MUST pass round the central markings at a mini-roundabout, except large vehicles that are physically unable to. Approach it in the same way as a normal roundabout.

q: You're approaching a double mini-roundabout. How should you deal with it?
options: Treat it as one large roundabout
Give way only at the first one
Treat each roundabout separately
Give way to traffic from the left
explain: At double mini-roundabouts you should treat each roundabout separately and give way to traffic from the right.

q: You're approaching a roundabout in an unfamiliar town. When should you decide which exit you need?
options: When you reach the give way line
As early as possible
Once you're on the roundabout
As you pass the exit before it
explain: On the approach to a roundabout, decide as early as possible which exit you need, give an appropriate signal and get into the correct lane.

q: You're approaching a junction with this sign and a solid white line across the road. You can see that the main road is clear. What must you do?
options: Slow down and drive on if it's clear
Stop only if traffic is coming
Stop behind the line, then go when safe
Stop with your front wheels on the line
explain: At a 'Stop' sign with a solid white line across the road you MUST stop behind the line, even if the road looks clear. Wait for a safe gap in the traffic before you move off.

q: You're about to emerge from a side road. There are broken white lines like these across the end of it. What must you do?
options: Give way to traffic on the main road
Stop, even if the road is clear
Expect main-road traffic to let you out
Give way only to traffic from the left
explain: You MUST give way to traffic on the main road when emerging from a junction with broken white lines across the road. Only pull out when there's a safe gap.

q: You're turning left into a side road. There's a bus lane on your left, and a bus is coming up in it from behind. What should you do?
options: Turn across the lane quickly
Stop in the bus lane and wait
Give way to the bus
Signal and expect the bus to stop
explain: When turning, keep as close to the left as is safe and give way to any vehicles using a bus lane, cycle lane, cycle track or tramway from either direction.

q: You're on a main road and want to turn right into a side road. There's no space marked for traffic turning right. Where should you position your car?
options: Just left of the middle of the road
Close to the left-hand kerb
On the right-hand side of the road
Straddling the centre line
explain: Well before you turn right, check your mirrors, give a right-turn signal and take up a position just left of the middle of the road. Leave room for other vehicles to pass on the left if possible.

q: You're waiting at traffic lights to go straight ahead across a box junction like this. The lights are green but your exit road is blocked. What should you do?
options: Enter the box and wait there
Sound your horn at the traffic ahead
Wait until your exit road is clear
Enter if the traffic ahead is moving
explain: You MUST NOT enter a box junction until your exit road or lane is clear. The only exception is when you're turning right and are stopped only by oncoming traffic or other vehicles waiting to turn right.

q: You're driving through a housing estate and approach crossroads with no signs or road markings. Who has priority?
options: Traffic coming from the right
Traffic on the wider road
Vehicles going straight ahead
Nobody has priority
explain: At unmarked junctions nobody has priority. Look all around before emerging, and only cross when there's a gap large enough to do so safely.

q: You're approaching a mini-roundabout. Compared with a normal roundabout, what should you remember?
options: You don't need to signal at all
Traffic from the left has priority
Cars may drive over the centre
There's less space and time to signal
explain: Approach a mini-roundabout in the same way as a normal roundabout, but remember there's less space to manoeuvre and less time to signal. All vehicles MUST pass round the central markings, except large vehicles that can't.

q: You're towing a trailer and want to turn right across a dual carriageway. The central reservation isn't deep enough for the length of your car and trailer. What should you do?
options: Wait in the central gap, partly blocking a lane
Wait until you can cross both halves in one go
Cross the first half, then stop in the right lane
Switch on your hazard lights and edge out
explain: Before crossing or turning right onto a dual carriageway, check whether the central reservation is deep enough to protect the full length of your vehicle. If it's too shallow, wait until you can cross both carriageways in one go.

q: You're crossing a dual carriageway from a side road. The central reservation is deep enough to protect your whole car. Where should you wait for a gap in the traffic on the second half?
options: In the right-hand lane of the first half
Just over the give way line of the second half
On the grass verge beside the main road
In the central reservation
explain: If the central reservation is deep enough to protect the full length of your vehicle, treat each half of the dual carriageway as a separate road. Wait in the central reservation until there's a safe gap on the second half.

q: You're approaching traffic lights that have been green for some time. They change to amber. When may you carry on?
options: If you can get through before red
If no pedestrians are waiting
If stopping might cause a collision
If the road beyond is clear
explain: Amber means stop at the stop line. You may go on only if you've already crossed the stop line or are so close to it that stopping might cause a collision.

q: You're waiting at a red traffic light. A green arrow pointing right lights up alongside it, as shown. You want to turn right. What does the green arrow mean?
options: You must wait for the full green light
You may go right if the way is clear
You may go in any direction if clear
You must wait until the red goes out
explain: A green arrow means you may go in the direction it shows, if the way is clear, whatever other lights are showing. Give other traffic, especially cyclists, time and room to move into the correct lane.

q: You're approaching traffic lights and want to go straight ahead. The left-hand lane is a filter lane with a green arrow pointing left. What should you do?
options: Keep out of the filter lane
Use the filter lane to pass the queue
Use it, then move right at the junction
Wait in the filter lane for full green
explain: A green filter arrow indicates a filter lane only. Don't enter that lane unless you want to go in the direction of the arrow.

q: You're approaching a junction with an advanced stop line for cyclists. The lights turn red before you reach the first white line. Where must you stop?
options: At the second white line
At the first white line
In the cyclists' waiting area
As close to the lights as possible
explain: You MUST stop at the first white line if the lights are amber or red, and avoid encroaching on the area marked for cyclists. You only stop at the second line if you'd already crossed the first when the lights turned red.

q: You're approaching a junction where the traffic lights aren't working. What should you do?
options: Assume you have priority if going straight
Wait until the lights are working again
Sound your horn and drive straight on
Treat it as an unmarked junction
explain: If the traffic lights aren't working, treat the situation as you would an unmarked junction, where nobody has priority, and proceed with great care.

q: You're behind a slow-moving car on a road with double white lines like these. The line nearest to you is solid. What should you do?
options: Overtake if the road ahead is clear
Overtake if it's doing under 30 mph
Stay behind the car
Straddle the lines to see ahead
explain: You MUST NOT overtake if you'd have to cross or straddle double white lines with a solid line nearest to you. The exceptions are passing a stationary vehicle, or overtaking a cycle, horse or road maintenance vehicle travelling at 10 mph or less.

q: You're following a slow tractor along a country road. Where should you NOT overtake it?
options: On a straight road with a clear view
Where the road ahead is wide and empty
Where you can see a long way ahead
Approaching the brow of a hill
explain: Don't overtake if there's any doubt, or where you can't see far enough ahead to be sure it's safe, such as when approaching a bend, a hump bridge or the brow of a hill.

q: You're driving along a single carriageway road. When may you overtake the vehicle in front on the left?
options: When it's signalling right and there's room
When it's travelling below the speed limit
When its driver waves you through
When it's slowing for a hazard ahead
explain: You should only overtake on the left if the vehicle in front is signalling to turn right and there's room to do so.

q: You need to stop briefly to let a passenger out. The only space is a taxi bay shown by signs and road markings. What does the law say?
options: You MUST NOT stop or park in it
You may stop to set down a passenger
You may stop there for up to 2 minutes
You may stop there outside rush hour
explain: You MUST NOT stop or park in taxi bays, as indicated by upright signs and markings. Find a safe, legal place to stop instead.

q: You want to overtake a slow vehicle, but you'd have to drive in a bus lane during its hours of operation. What does the law say?
options: You may if no buses are coming
You MUST NOT overtake
You may if it's only for a short way
You may if you signal first
explain: You MUST NOT overtake if you would have to enter a lane reserved for buses, trams or cycles during its hours of operation.

q: You're parking in a residential street near a junction. There are no marked parking spaces. You shouldn't park within what distance of the junction?
options: 5 metres (16 feet)
15 metres (49 feet)
10 metres (32 feet)
20 metres (66 feet)
explain: Don't stop or park opposite or within 10 metres (32 feet) of a junction, except in an authorised parking space.

q: You want to drop off a passenger close to a zebra crossing. There are white zig-zag lines on the approach to it. What's the rule?
options: You must not stop or park on them
You may stop briefly to let them out
You may park there for up to 2 minutes
You may stop if you switch on hazard lights
explain: You MUST NOT stop or park on a pedestrian crossing or in the area marked by the zig-zag lines. Find a safe and legal place further away.

q: You've found a parking space on the road, but it's directly opposite a traffic island. What should you do?
options: Park there with your hazard lights on
Park there, as it isn't a junction
Find somewhere else to park
Park partly on the pavement instead
explain: Don't stop or park opposite a traffic island. Other places to avoid include bends, near the brow of a hill and within 10 metres of a junction, except in an authorised parking space.

q: You're collecting a friend in town and need to stop for a few minutes. Which of these places should you avoid?
options: A marked parking bay
An off-street car park
Near a bus stop
A lay-by
explain: Don't stop or park at or near a bus or tram stop or taxi rank. Use off-street parking areas or marked parking bays wherever possible.

q: You've found a space to park, but the kerb there has been lowered to help wheelchair users. What should you do?
options: Park there, as it's easy to get out
Find somewhere else to park
Park there for a few minutes only
Park there if you're not blocking traffic
explain: Don't stop or park where the kerb has been lowered to help wheelchair users and powered mobility vehicles. In Scotland you MUST NOT park where the kerb has been lowered to help pedestrians or cyclists.

q: You're driving in London and the only space you can find is partly on the pavement. What's the rule?
options: You must not park partly or wholly on it
You may park with two wheels on it
You may park there for up to 30 minutes
You may park there with hazards on
explain: You MUST NOT park partially or wholly on the pavement in London or Scotland, except in limited circumstances. Pavement parking can seriously inconvenience pedestrians, wheelchair users and people with prams or pushchairs.

q: You're parking on a road at night. You're not in a recognised parking space. What must you NOT do?
options: Park close to the kerb on your side
Park facing against the traffic flow
Park under or near a street light
Switch off your headlights and engine
explain: You MUST NOT park on a road at night facing against the direction of the traffic flow unless you're in a recognised parking space.

q: You park your car at night in a lay-by on a road with a 50 mph speed limit. What must you do?
options: Leave your parking lights on
Switch off all your lights
Leave your dipped headlights on
Leave your hazard lights flashing
explain: All vehicles MUST display parking lights when parked on a road, or in a lay-by on a road, with a speed limit greater than 30 mph.

q: You're leaving your car overnight on a road with a 30 mph limit. It isn't in a parking place or lay-by. Where may you leave it without lights?
options: Within 10 metres of a junction, close to the kerb
At least 10 metres from a junction, facing against the traffic
At least 10 metres from a junction, facing with the traffic
Anywhere under a street light, facing either way
explain: On a road with a speed limit of 30 mph or less, a car may be parked without lights if it's at least 10 metres (32 feet) from any junction, close to the kerb and facing in the direction of the traffic flow.

q: You're driving along a main road and pass this sign. What does it tell you that you must NOT do?
options: Stop on the road
Overtake other vehicles
Drive faster than 30 mph
Turn into side roads
explain: This sign means no stopping (clearway). You MUST NOT stop or park on a clearway.

q: You're driving through a town centre and see this sign. During the times shown, when may you stop on this road?
options: To load or unload goods from a van
For up to 20 minutes if you stay with it
Whenever you can find a free space
Only to set down or pick up passengers
explain: On an urban clearway you MUST NOT stop within its hours of operation, except for as long as necessary to pick up or set down passengers.

q: You see this sign by some parking bays. You don't have a permit. What should you do?
options: Park for up to 20 minutes
Park if you're only loading
Park if the bays are empty
Park somewhere else
explain: You MUST NOT park in parking spaces reserved for specific users, such as permit holders, residents, Blue Badge holders or motorcycles, unless you're entitled to do so.

q: You realise you're going the wrong way along a busy main road. What's the safest way to turn round?
options: Make a U-turn across the main road
Do a three-point turn in the main road
Reverse back along the main road
Drive round a block of side streets
explain: If you need to turn your vehicle round, wait until you find a safe place. Try not to reverse or turn round in a busy road; find a quiet side road or drive round a block of side streets.

q: You're about to park on your driveway, which opens onto a busy road. What does the Highway Code advise?
options: Drive in and reverse out later
Reverse in so you can drive out
Drive in and turn round in the road
Whichever way is quickest for you
explain: When using a driveway, reverse in and drive out if you can. You also shouldn't reverse from a side road into a main road.

q: You're reversing your car into a quiet side road. How far are you allowed to reverse?
options: No further than necessary
No more than 10 metres
As far as you like if it's clear
No more than two car lengths
explain: You MUST NOT reverse your vehicle further than necessary. Look all around before and while reversing, and give way to any pedestrians who may be crossing.

q: You've missed your turning and are approaching a mini-roundabout. You're thinking of making a U-turn there. What does the Highway Code advise?
options: U-turns are best made at mini-roundabouts
Only make a U-turn if you signal right
Avoid making U-turns at mini-roundabouts
U-turns are fine if you drive over the centre
explain: Avoid making U-turns at mini-roundabouts, where there's less space to manoeuvre and less time to signal. Beware of other drivers doing this.

q: You're waiting at a level crossing. A train passes, but the red lights keep flashing. What must you do?
options: Cross, as the train has passed
Keep waiting, as another train is coming
Zig-zag round the barriers if it's clear
Phone the signal operator, then cross
explain: You MUST wait if a train goes by and the red lights continue to flash. This means another train will be passing soon. Only cross when the lights go off and the barriers open.

q: You're driving over a level crossing. You've just crossed the white line when the amber light comes on. What should you do?
options: Stop on the crossing and wait
Reverse back behind the white line
Keep going and clear the crossing
Stop and switch on hazard lights
explain: Keep going if you've already crossed the white line when the amber light comes on. Don't reverse onto or over a controlled crossing.

q: You're driving on a single carriageway road that has four lanes. Which lanes should you use?
options: Only those signs or markings show
Any lane that's clear of traffic
The two lanes nearest the kerb
Whichever lane is moving fastest
explain: Where a single carriageway has four or more lanes, use only the lanes that signs or markings indicate.

q: You come to a level crossing with user-operated gates and small red and green lights. When may you cross?
options: When the red light is showing
When you can't see a train coming
After sounding your horn twice
Only when the green light is on
explain: You MUST NOT cross when the red light is showing; only cross if the green light is on. Open the gates on both sides, check the green light is still on, cross quickly and close the gates when you're clear.

q: Traffic is moving slowly over a level crossing ahead of you. The road on the far side is congested. What should you do?
options: Follow the car in front closely
Wait until it's clear on the other side
Stop on the crossing if the lights are off
Drive onto the crossing and wait there
explain: Never drive onto a level crossing until the road is clear on the other side, and don't get too close to the car in front. Never stop or park on, or near, a crossing.

q: You're approaching a zebra crossing. A pedestrian is waiting on the pavement to cross. What should you do?
options: Wave them across in front of you
Flash your headlights at them
Sound your horn to warn them
Slow down and give way to them
explain: Be ready to slow down or stop, and give way to pedestrians waiting to cross. Don't wave, flash your lights or use your horn to invite them across, as this could be dangerous if another vehicle is approaching.

q: You've stopped at a pelican crossing. The red light changes to flashing amber. What does this mean?
options: You must wait for the green light
It's about to change back to red
You may go if the crossing is clear
Pedestrians must now give way to you
explain: At a pelican crossing, flashing amber follows the red light. You MUST give way to any pedestrians on the crossing, but if there's no one on it you may proceed with caution.

q: You've overtaken using the right-hand lane of a three-lane dual carriageway. What should you do next?
options: Stay in the right-hand lane
Return to the middle, then the left lane
Cut straight across to the left lane
Stay in the middle lane from now on
explain: On a dual carriageway with three or more lanes, you may use the middle lanes or the right-hand lane to overtake, but you should return to the middle lanes and then the left-hand lane when it's safe.

q: When are you allowed to drive on or over a pavement?
options: To get past a queue of traffic
To let a bus pass on a narrow road
To reach a property or in an emergency
To park there for a short time
explain: You MUST NOT drive on or over a pavement, footpath or bridleway except to gain lawful access to property, or in the case of an emergency.

q: You're approaching a puffin crossing, but its lights aren't working. What should you do?
options: Drive through, as it's out of use
Expect pedestrians to wait for you
Stop and wait until it's repaired
Proceed with extreme caution
explain: If a signal-controlled crossing isn't working, proceed with extreme caution. Don't enter the crossing if you can't completely clear it.

q: You want to pull up on the left just after a side road. When should you signal left?
options: As you're passing the side road
Before you reach the side road
Only after you've stopped
There's no need to signal
explain: Make sure your signals won't confuse others. If you want to stop after a side road, don't signal until you're passing it; signalling earlier may make others think you're turning into it.

q: You're on a busy road and have signalled to move into the next lane. What should you remember?
options: Other drivers must now let you in
You needn't check your mirrors again
You should leave your signal on afterwards
Your signal doesn't give you priority
explain: Signalling doesn't give you priority. Only move over when it's safe, and cancel your signal after use.

q: Road markings show that you can join a roundabout without giving way. What should you still do?
options: Look to the right before joining
Stop at the line before joining
Sound your horn as you join
Signal left as you join
explain: Check whether road markings allow you to enter the roundabout without giving way. If so, proceed, but still look to the right before joining.

q: A police car behind you is flashing its blue lights, and the officer points for you to pull over. What must you do?
options: Stop straight away, wherever you are
Stop when safe and turn off the engine
Speed up so the police car can pass
Keep going until you find a car park
explain: If the police want to stop your vehicle, you MUST pull over and stop as soon as it's safe to do so. Then switch off your engine.

q: A vehicle in front of you is flashing amber lights. A Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) officer in it is signalling for you to follow. What should you do?
options: Overtake it as soon as it's safe
Ignore it, as only police can stop you
Follow it to a safe place to stop
Stop immediately in the road
explain: DVSA officers have the power to stop vehicles on all roads. Flashing amber lights from the front mean they want you to follow them to a safe place to stop, and it's an offence not to comply.

q: You're driving on a motorway in England. Uniformed traffic officers want to stop you because your roof load looks insecure. How will they usually attract your attention?
options: Flashing blue lights and sounding a siren
Flashing amber lights, usually from behind
Flashing green lights from in front of you
A red flag waved from the hard shoulder
explain: Traffic officers can stop vehicles on most motorways and some 'A' class roads in England and Wales. They'll usually flash amber lights from behind and direct you to pull over; you MUST then stop when it's safe and switch off your engine.
